lseek(2)                                                     System Calls Manual                                                    lseek(2)

NAME
       lseek - reposition read/write file offset

LIBRARY
       Standard C library (libc, -lc)

SYNOPSIS
       #include <unistd.h>

       off_t lseek(int fd, off_t offset, int whence);

DESCRIPTION
       lseek()  repositions  the  file offset of the open file description associated with the file descriptor fd to the argument offset ac‐
       cording to the directive whence as follows:

       SEEK_SET
              The file offset is set to offset bytes.

       SEEK_CUR
              The file offset is set to its current location plus offset bytes.

       SEEK_END
              The file offset is set to the size of the file plus offset bytes.

       lseek() allows the file offset to be set beyond the end of the file (but this does not change the size of  the  file).   If  data  is
       later written at this point, subsequent reads of the data in the gap (a "hole") return null bytes ('\0') until data is actually writ‐
       ten into the gap.

   Seeking file data and holes
       Since Linux 3.1, Linux supports the following additional values for whence:

       SEEK_DATA
              Adjust  the file offset to the next location in the file greater than or equal to offset containing data.  If offset points to
              data, then the file offset is set to offset.

       SEEK_HOLE
              Adjust the file offset to the next hole in the file greater than or equal to offset.  If offset points into the  middle  of  a
              hole,  then the file offset is set to offset.  If there is no hole past offset, then the file offset is adjusted to the end of
              the file (i.e., there is an implicit hole at the end of any file).

       In both of the above cases, lseek() fails if offset points past the end of the file.

       These operations allow applications to map holes in a sparsely allocated file.  This can be useful  for  applications  such  as  file
       backup tools, which can save space when creating backups and preserve holes, if they have a mechanism for discovering holes.

       For  the  purposes  of  these operations, a hole is a sequence of zeros that (normally) has not been allocated in the underlying file
       storage.  However, a filesystem is not obliged to report holes, so these operations are not a guaranteed mechanism  for  mapping  the
       storage space actually allocated to a file.  (Furthermore, a sequence of zeros that actually has been written to the underlying stor‐
       age  may not be reported as a hole.)  In the simplest implementation, a filesystem can support the operations by making SEEK_HOLE al‐
       ways return the offset of the end of the file, and making SEEK_DATA always return offset (i.e., even if the location referred  to  by
       offset is a hole, it can be considered to consist of data that is a sequence of zeros).

       The _GNU_SOURCE feature test macro must be defined in order to obtain the definitions of SEEK_DATA and SEEK_HOLE from <unistd.h>.

       The SEEK_HOLE and SEEK_DATA operations are supported for the following filesystems:

       •  Btrfs (since Linux 3.1)

       •  OCFS (since Linux 3.2)

       •  XFS (since Linux 3.5)

       •  ext4 (since Linux 3.8)

       •  tmpfs(5) (since Linux 3.8)

       •  NFS (since Linux 3.18)

       •  FUSE (since Linux 4.5)

       •  GFS2 (since Linux 4.15)

RETURN VALUE
       Upon  successful  completion,  lseek() returns the resulting offset location as measured in bytes from the beginning of the file.  On
       error, the value (off_t) -1 is returned and errno is set to indicate the error.

ERRORS
       EBADF  fd is not an open file descriptor.

       EINVAL whence is not valid.  Or: the resulting file offset would be negative, or beyond the end of a seekable device.

       ENXIO  whence is SEEK_DATA or SEEK_HOLE, and offset is beyond the end of the file, or whence is SEEK_DATA and offset is within a hole
              at the end of the file.

       EOVERFLOW
              The resulting file offset cannot be represented in an off_t.

       ESPIPE fd is associated with a pipe, socket, or FIFO.

VERSIONS
       On Linux, using lseek() on a terminal device fails with the error ESPIPE.

STANDARDS
       POSIX.1-2008.

HISTORY
       POSIX.1-2001, SVr4, 4.3BSD.

       SEEK_DATA and SEEK_HOLE are nonstandard extensions also present in Solaris, FreeBSD, and DragonFly BSD; they are proposed for  inclu‐
       sion in the next POSIX revision (Issue 8).

NOTES
       See open(2) for a discussion of the relationship between file descriptors, open file descriptions, and files.

       If  the O_APPEND file status flag is set on the open file description, then a write(2) always moves the file offset to the end of the
       file, regardless of the use of lseek().

       Some devices are incapable of seeking and POSIX does not specify which devices must support lseek().

SEE ALSO
       dup(2), fallocate(2), fork(2), open(2), fseek(3), lseek64(3), posix_fallocate(3)

NAME
       lseek - reposition read/write file offset

LIBRARY
       Standard C library (libc, -lc)

SYNOPSIS
       #include <unistd.h>

       off_t lseek(int fd, off_t offset, int whence);

DESCRIPTION
       lseek()  repositions  the  file offset of the open file description associated with the file descriptor fd to the argument offset ac‐
       cording to the directive whence as follows:

       SEEK_SET
              The file offset is set to offset bytes.

       SEEK_CUR
              The file offset is set to its current location plus offset bytes.

       SEEK_END
              The file offset is set to the size of the file plus offset bytes.

       lseek() allows the file offset to be set beyond the end of the file (but this does not change the size of  the  file).   If  data  is
       later written at this point, subsequent reads of the data in the gap (a "hole") return null bytes ('\0') until data is actually writ‐
       ten into the gap.

   Seeking file data and holes
       Since Linux 3.1, Linux supports the following additional values for whence:

       SEEK_DATA
              Adjust  the file offset to the next location in the file greater than or equal to offset containing data.  If offset points to
              data, then the file offset is set to offset.

       SEEK_HOLE
              Adjust the file offset to the next hole in the file greater than or equal to offset.  If offset points into the  middle  of  a
              hole,  then the file offset is set to offset.  If there is no hole past offset, then the file offset is adjusted to the end of
              the file (i.e., there is an implicit hole at the end of any file).

       In both of the above cases, lseek() fails if offset points past the end of the file.

       These operations allow applications to map holes in a sparsely allocated file.  This can be useful  for  applications  such  as  file
       backup tools, which can save space when creating backups and preserve holes, if they have a mechanism for discovering holes.

       For  the  purposes  of  these operations, a hole is a sequence of zeros that (normally) has not been allocated in the underlying file
       storage.  However, a filesystem is not obliged to report holes, so these operations are not a guaranteed mechanism  for  mapping  the
       storage space actually allocated to a file.  (Furthermore, a sequence of zeros that actually has been written to the underlying stor‐
       age  may not be reported as a hole.)  In the simplest implementation, a filesystem can support the operations by making SEEK_HOLE al‐
       ways return the offset of the end of the file, and making SEEK_DATA always return offset (i.e., even if the location referred  to  by
       offset is a hole, it can be considered to consist of data that is a sequence of zeros).

       The _GNU_SOURCE feature test macro must be defined in order to obtain the definitions of SEEK_DATA and SEEK_HOLE from <unistd.h>.

       The SEEK_HOLE and SEEK_DATA operations are supported for the following filesystems:

       •  Btrfs (since Linux 3.1)

       •  OCFS (since Linux 3.2)

       •  XFS (since Linux 3.5)

       •  ext4 (since Linux 3.8)

       •  tmpfs(5) (since Linux 3.8)

       •  NFS (since Linux 3.18)

       •  FUSE (since Linux 4.5)

       •  GFS2 (since Linux 4.15)

RETURN VALUE
       Upon  successful  completion,  lseek() returns the resulting offset location as measured in bytes from the beginning of the file.  On
       error, the value (off_t) -1 is returned and errno is set to indicate the error.

ERRORS
       EBADF  fd is not an open file descriptor.

       EINVAL whence is not valid.  Or: the resulting file offset would be negative, or beyond the end of a seekable device.

       ENXIO  whence is SEEK_DATA or SEEK_HOLE, and offset is beyond the end of the file, or whence is SEEK_DATA and offset is within a hole
              at the end of the file.

       EOVERFLOW
              The resulting file offset cannot be represented in an off_t.

       ESPIPE fd is associated with a pipe, socket, or FIFO.

VERSIONS
       On Linux, using lseek() on a terminal device fails with the error ESPIPE.

STANDARDS
       POSIX.1-2008.

HISTORY
       POSIX.1-2001, SVr4, 4.3BSD.

       SEEK_DATA and SEEK_HOLE are nonstandard extensions also present in Solaris, FreeBSD, and DragonFly BSD; they are proposed for  inclu‐
       sion in the next POSIX revision (Issue 8).

NOTES
       See open(2) for a discussion of the relationship between file descriptors, open file descriptions, and files.

       If  the O_APPEND file status flag is set on the open file description, then a write(2) always moves the file offset to the end of the
       file, regardless of the use of lseek().

       Some devices are incapable of seeking and POSIX does not specify which devices must support lseek().

SEE ALSO
       dup(2), fallocate(2), fork(2), open(2), fseek(3), lseek64(3), posix_fallocate(3)

I wrote the summary to `summaries/obtained/lseek/lseek.c`. It compiles with the command you gave, with no warnings even under `-Wall`. I haven't run it against the real `lseek` through the fuzzing setup in `config.yaml`, so its behaviour is untested.

**How it works**
- **`whence`:** each of `SEEK_SET`, `SEEK_CUR` and `SEEK_END` gets its own path, starting from 0, the current offset or the file size, plus `offset`. Any other value returns -1 (EINVAL).
- **Negative position:** one `pos < 0` check returns -1 (EINVAL). Because `off_t` is 32-bit under `-m32` and the starting point is never negative, a sum that overflows wraps to a negative number. So the same check also covers EOVERFLOW without an extra branch.
- **Bad descriptor:** there's no separate check. When `fd` isn't open, the file functions return -1 and `__file_set_offset` fails. A descriptor of the form `ite(cond, fd, -1)` is passed through unchanged, so its failure case ends up inside the result as `ite(cond, pos, -1)` without splitting the path.
- **Concrete position:** `__file_set_offset` needs a concrete value, but `offset` has no bounds. So when the position is symbolic, I pick one possible value and add the constraint that it equals that value. As a result, each path tests only one offset.

**A choice that differs from your config:** `argspec.yaml` calls `whence = 3` "invalid", but on Linux 3 is `SEEK_DATA` (and 4 is `SEEK_HOLE`). The real `lseek` will handle 3 as `SEEK_DATA`, so I modelled both instead of returning EINVAL:
- If `offset` is negative or at or past the file size, they fail (ENXIO).
- Otherwise `SEEK_DATA` stays at `offset` and `SEEK_HOLE` moves to the end of the file. This treats the file as having no holes except the implicit one at its end, which the man page allows.
- The two bounds are joined with a bitwise `|` rather than `||`, so they make one branch instead of two.

If your test harness really expects 3 to be rejected, delete the `SEEK_DATA`/`SEEK_HOLE` block.

"""Sampling where the fuzzer will not go: one input per unexercised path.

distinguishes three ranges of an argument the function treats uniformly gets
one input from the campaign and two paths nothing ever tried -- and a path no
sample reaches is a path no sample can contradict. That is a silent gap, not a
visible one: the run reports `passed`.

the formula mentions. This closes the loop afterwards, against the samples the
campaign actually produced:

    1. for each stored path of the summary, does any sample reach it?
    2. for one that has none, ask the solver for an input that does
    3. run the concrete function on that input, and record what it returned
    4. repeat, with the inputs already tried blocked, until every path has been
       reached or the budget runs out

the summary and the answer comes from the implementation, so a path the summary
invented -- one admitting inputs on which the function does something else --
is refuted by the very input built to reach it. That is the over-approximation
direction, and it is the one a coverage-guided campaign is worst at finding.

`check_sample`, run on a real execution of the real function; what this changes
is only which executions happen. An input that misses the path it was aimed at

input the test's own bounds turn away is recorded as rejected, as any other

    def lift_fds(self) -> Bool:
        """
        Lifts each open descriptor: its flags (those it keeps, KEPT_FLAGS)
        and offset, and the mode, size and bytes of its file, as seen
        through it.

        Besides the per-fd variables, `file_open_fds` is a bit mask of the
        descriptors open at this point (bit N for fd N). It describes the
        whole set in one variable, so a descriptor that one side has open and
        the other does not is a mismatch, instead of leaving that descriptor's
        variables unconstrained.
        """

        int_size = self.state.arch.sizeof["int"]
        char_size = 8
        fd_cases = []
        open_mask = BVV(0, OPEN_FDS_BITS)

        for fd, fde in self.fds.items():
            open_mask += self.open_bit(fd, fde)

            prefix = f"file_fd{fd}"

            flags = self.sym_var(f"{prefix}_flags", int_size)
            metadata = flags == self.bvv_int(fde.flags & KEPT_FLAGS)

            file_cases = []

            for entry in fde.entries:
                bytes = []

                mode = self.sym_var(f"{prefix}_mode", int_size)
                offset = self.sym_var(f"{prefix}_offset", int_size)
                size = self.sym_var(f"{prefix}_size", int_size)
                file_bytes = entry.file.bytes

                for i, c in enumerate(file_bytes):
                    c = self.bvv_char(c)
                    byte = self.sym_var(f"{prefix}_byte_{i}", char_size)
                    bytes.append(byte == c)

                    mode == self.bvv_int(entry.file.mode),
                    offset == self.bvv_int(entry.offset),

**Why it can't pass as configured:** the engine keeps each descriptor's file offset as a single fixed number on every path. `__file_set_offset` rejects an offset that can take more than one value, and `lift_fds` in `src/summboundverify/validation_tool/se/api/functions/fs/symbolic/fs.py:647` records `entry.offset` as a constant. So each path ends with one fixed file offset, and covering every offset would need one path per value. `argspec.yaml` leaves `offset` unbounded, so any open-descriptor sample with a different offset is rejected. Your sample (offset 0x2100, returning 0x2100) is one of those.

**What I changed** in `summaries/obtained/lseek/lseek.c`:
- **Few possible positions:** when the open descriptor can reach at most 65 positions (`MAX_FORKS` 64), the summary forks once per value, following the `fork_bounded` template. This is exact, so with a bounded `offset` it accepts every valid sample.
- **More positions:** the summary falls back to the previous behaviour and picks one value. It still leaves `offset` free when the descriptor isn't open.
- **Unopened descriptor:** a descriptor that is definitely not open now returns -1 straight away.

**To get a pass, one of these has to change**, and both are your call:
1. **Bound `offset` in `argspec.yaml`**, e.g. a small `maxvalue` such as 16. Per the comment in that file, this stops negative offsets from being tested, which is why it was left unbounded.
2. **Let the engine keep a symbolic file offset.** `__file_set_offset` would need to accept a symbolic value and `lift_fds` would need to record it. The summary could then set the exact position and drop the forking.

The only summary-side workaround is the one I mentioned last time: return the exact position while setting the file to a different value. That would hide the mismatch only because the reported offset would be wrong, so I haven't done it.
